title: The Boat, Not The Brain
concept: A robot that finds the brain of each individual salmon is real and independently reported. Its arrival in Alaska is one trade write-up. The film separates the two on screen.

angle.thesis: The hard part of putting a robot on a fishing boat is already solved, and it is not the part anyone expects. The unsolved part is the boat.
angle.long_form: A machine learning model finds the brain of each individual salmon, because the brain sits in a different place in every fish, which is why a jig cannot do this and a model must. That is real and was independently reported twice. What is not established is that any of it has reached Alaska. One trade write-up carries the entire Cook Inlet story, against more than thirteen hundred permits in that inlet alone.
angle.valence_defense: Celebratory would overclaim an Alaska deployment nobody has confirmed. Cautionary would undersell engineering that two independent outlets verified two years apart. Curiosity is the only register that can hold a solved mechanism and an unconfirmed rollout at the same time, and it rotates off a wry run and a mixed one.
supporting_facts: c9 + c18: computer vision and machine learning locate the brain of each individual fish. Khawaja, verbatim: the brain can be in a different location. That sentence is the whole reason a model is needed.

c15 + c14: the company's own 2024 goal was ten machines in use company-wide, across all fisheries. Upper Cook Inlet alone holds more than 1,300 permits, about a tenth of every salmon permit in Alaska.
c19: exactly one trade write-up carries the Alaska story. No Alaska outlet and no fisheries trade outlet has covered it.
angle.fair_counterpoint_that_gets_a_scene: This is exactly what a real pilot looks like on day one. One boat, one write-up, proof before scale. Demanding fleet-wide numbers from a seed-stage company's first Alaska mention is an unfair bar, and every genuine rollout in this fishery's history started smaller than its press release.
angle.how_it_narrows_honestly: The film does not call the Alaska claim false. It says the record is one write-up, names what would settle it, and leaves the question open on screen.
angle.the_lazy_angle_we_refuse: Robot comes for Alaska's fishermen. It is wrong on the facts: ike jime needs a trained hand and most small boats do not do it at all, so no job is being displaced. A skill that mostly was not there is being made reachable.
angle.who_it_serves: A Cook Inlet permit holder who heard this secondhand now knows which half is engineering and which half is a press release, and what question to ask before believing it applies to their boat.
runners_up: SKEPTIC lens, pure sourcing story: rejected as the spine because a film whose subject is the thinness of a press release has no second movement and no mechanism to draw.
ENTHUSIAST lens, quality-at-capture as a small-boat lever: kept and grafted into Act 2, because it is the honest reason an Alaskan should care at all.
MECHANISM lens, automating access to a scarce hand skill: kept and grafted, and it supplies the refusal of the job-loss frame.
angle.throughline_object: THE TARGET DOT, the point the machine picks behind a salmon's eye

treatment.winner: THE ENTHUSIAST, 'The Boat, Not the Brain'
treatment.judge_reasoning: It had the only cold open that is a held breath rather than an explainer, the strongest turn (the reticle pulls back to a dozen visibly different hulls and fits none of them, which is the thesis as a picture), and a throughline that starts as a human grease-pencil X and ends as a machine mark, so the object carries the argument instead of decorating it. Its button returns to the exact opening frame with the spike now carrying the mark, which is a real bookend and not a restatement.
grafts: From THE EXPLAINER: the JIG versus MODEL cutaway, with a fixed guide coming down dead straight and landing beside the mark. It is the single best explanatory beat the room produced and it earns the machine-learning claim visually instead of asserting it.
From THE EXPLAINER: the blank price tag for 'no dollar figure exists anywhere', which turns a sourcing limit into a picture.
From THE DRAMATIST: holding the 'one trade write-up, no Alaska outlet' beat long enough to read twice, rather than passing over it.
From THE DRAMATIST: the empty-masthead rack as the visual form of that absence.
treatment.lenses_run: Dramatist, Explainer, Enthusiast. The Comedian lens was deliberately not convened: the subject is the killing of animals for food quality, and a lens briefed to pitch for laughs would have produced material this film could not use without being disrespectful of both the fish and the fishermen. Logged for Phase 8.

retention_plan.the_test: Act 3, 68.4 to 96.8s. The fair case for patience gets the widest, warmest, emptiest shot in the film (S9), a single boat at a single dock in a big dawn inlet, and the CTO's verbatim line is allowed to sit with the bed dipped and nothing competing. It is staged as the film's most beautiful shot on purpose, because a counter-argument that is staged uglier than the thesis is a strawman.
retention_plan.throughline_object: THE MARK. A human grease-pencil X, then a machine reticle, then ten lit marks, then a dotted mark that has not landed, then a mark that fits none of a dozen hulls, then finally settling on the spike from the opening frame.
retention_plan.the_two_loops: Primary: the spike hovers over the X at 7.6s and never descends, and the film does not resolve what lands on the fish until the mark settles onto the spike itself at 116.8s. Secondary: the dotted unlit machine outline settles on Cook Inlet at 56.4s and stays dotted until the NO BOAT COUNT stamp at 93.2s.
retention_plan.padding_test: Every Act 3 beat was tested against a 90-second cut. The wide inlet establish earns its seconds because without a scale to land against, the ten-machines figure reads as a gotcha rather than an honest limit. The held CTO quote earns its seconds because cutting it short turns the fairest line in the fact set into a throwaway and makes the act a strawman. The empty masthead rack earns its seconds because 'no Alaska outlet has covered this' is the film's most important epistemic claim and a viewer who races past it remembers only the robot. The tipped FLEET NUMBERS bar earns its seconds because it is the film conceding a point, and a concession delivered in a clause is not a concession. Nothing in Act 3 restates Act 2.

divergence_note: This board is authored from scratch for this story and diverges hard from the last two dispatches, both of which were interiors lit by practical sources. 2026-08-05 was an eye-level naturalistic scene in a specimen room on a grid-modular layout with vertical descent, a single organic hero and a rise-reveal camera under overcast diffuse light, in cabinet green and bone with one teal. 2026-08-06 was an instrument-screen data-brutalist HUD frame with radial emanation, an instrument hero and a locked-drift camera under night practicals, in municipal slate-blue with signal orange. This film is an EXTERIOR at dawn on open water. Its point of view is macro-closeup on organic form rather than a screen or a room, its layout is a single object in deep negative space rather than a grid or a bezel, its motion is horizontal traverse across water rather than descent or emanation, its hero treatment is a multiplicity, a fleet and a permit field rather than one creature or one device, and its register is instrument-readout, a perception overlay laid over a real lit world, which is neither of the previous two. The palette shares no token with either. The spatial signature, macro-closeup on a single-object void moving horizontally, has not been used in the ledger window. The one axis it shares with 2026-08-05 is the rise-reveal camera, and it is earned here by a genuinely different move: that film rose from a specimen to a room, this one rises from one deck to a fleet of visibly mismatched hulls, which is the film's entire argument rather than a context shot.

hook.frame1: A chrome sockeye on a wet board at dawn, gold rim light on every scale, and a worn wooden spike held an inch above the spot behind its eye. Nothing has happened to the fish yet. It is the most finished thing this film will draw.
hook.headline: WHERE DOES A FISH KEEP ITS BRAIN
hook.loopback: The final beat returns to this exact frame, the same spike on the same board, with the small gold mark now resting on the spike's tip instead of the machine's screen.

throughline.object: THE MARK, the point chosen behind a salmon's eye

states.state: HUMAN. A wobbly grease-pencil X drawn by a gloved hand, irregular and made by eye.
MACHINE. A perfect cyan reticle inside the machine's view, snapping to a different true point on each of three fish.
DOTTED. An unlit outline settled over Cook Inlet that never fills in, because nothing has been confirmed.
WAITING. Through the whole fair-case act the mark is nowhere on screen, because the crate on the dock is still shut. Its absence is the state.
COUNTED. Ten small lit marks in a row, the company's own stated ambition, made countable.
HOMELESS. One lit mark hovering over a dozen visibly different hulls, fitting none of them.
RESTING. The mark settles onto the tip of the wooden spike from the opening frame, back where a human put it.

open_loop.what: The spike hovers an inch above the drawn X and does not descend. The film never shows a strike land on a fish. What finally lands, at the button, is the mark itself, settling onto the spike's tip.

open_loop_2.what: The announcement lands on Cook Inlet and the mark that arrives with it is DOTTED and unlit, a promise the film refuses to fill in. It is still dotted when the NO BOAT COUNT stamp lands at 106.6s, which is the answer to what it was waiting for.

reveals.what: three sockeye from directly above, the true point lighting in a visibly different place on each, with the wrong guesses ghosting out around them
the machine's view resolves as the four corner ticks converge onto the true point and the confidence bloom pulses once
a field of more than thirteen hundred permit tiles builds outward around the ten lit marks until the ten are a speck
THE SIGNATURE SHOT. The camera rises off one deck and keeps rising until a dozen visibly different hulls sit around it, and the mark fits none of them

audio_arc.note: The 76.2 dip is the film's held breath under the CTO quote, where the bed drops more than six dB and the water is the only thing left moving. The riser at 104 carries the permit field building. The real pre-button silence sits at 112.8 as the camera finishes its rise.
